newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian officer killed in breakaway Georgia region.
newsitem.headline: Russian officer killed in breakaway Georgia region.

text.p: A Russian army officer was killed and two other servicemen were badly wounded when an armoured car carrying peacekeeping troops hit a mine in Georgia's breakaway Abkhazia region, a Defence Ministry spokesman said on Tuesday.

The spokesman gave no details, but Interfax news agency said the incident occurred on Monday in the Gali region, where Russian troops control a buffer zone separating Georgia from its Black Sea province of Abkhazia.
The future of the force has been a source of growing irritation between Moscow and Georgia, raising the prospect that the troops could pull out and conflict could flare anew.

A security official in Abkhazia, which has run itself as a de facto independent state since driving Georgian forces out in 1993, called the blast a "terrorist act aimed at disrupting the peacekeeping operation".
He blamed "a sabotage group" from Georgia.
Avtandil Ioseliani, deputy security minister in the Georgian capital, Tbilisi, called such accusations "groundless".
"We do not need to stage sabotage acts against Russian peacekeepers," he told reporters in the capital Tbilisi. "They will leave if Georgia demands it."
Several Russian servicemen have been injured in similar incidents which the conflicting sides blamed on each other.
The explosion took place a day after a Russian sergeant shot dead 10 of his fellow servicemen in a peacekeeping unit in the Gali region and then killed himself.
The role of the Russian peacekeepers has become a contentious issue. Apart from peacekeepers, Russia has several military bases in Georgia under an inter-government agreement.
The Tbilisi government is demanding that the 2,500 peacekeepers take on a more aggressive and broader mandate, helping refugees from the region resettle.

The Georgian parliament passed a resolution last week seeking to end the Russian role in Abkhazia if no progress was made in bringing peace to the region by the end of the troops' current mandate on August 1.
Sergei Yastrzhembsky, press secretary to Russian President Boris Yeltsin, called that "political blackmail".

He was quoted on Monday as saying the Georgian parliament was "forcing us to rethink the advisability of the further presence of Russian peacekeepers in the conflict zone and the possibility of fulfilling their mandate".
Analysts say the departure of the peacekeepers could spark a renewal of fighting between the separatists and Georgian government forces. Nearly four years of peace talks have reached a dead end.
Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze last week offered a new start to peace negotiations, while ruling out any solution that recognised Abkhazia's independence.
But next day he also warned the separatists that they would be committing suicide if they chose to go to war again with a rebuilt Georgian army.
Russia's Interfax news agency said a round of talks between Abkhazia and Georgia would start on Wednesday in Moscow.
